cards.explanation: The answer is cancel. Moses, Israel's leader, says it plain: “At the end of every seven years you must cancel debts.” Seven years go by, and the lender lets go of what his neighbor owes him. A creditor in that land had a standing appointment to let things go.

The answer is that the LORD's time of release has been proclaimed. That's the reason in verse 2: “…because the LORD’s time of release has been proclaimed.” No loophole and no mood swing, because the lender lets it go when the LORD calls the time. I've been left in a drawer for years and never once got a notice that nice. Release means release, friends.

The answer is False. Verse 3 says, “You may collect something from a foreigner, but you must forgive whatever your brother owes you.” The release is for the debts of a brother. A foreigner's debt isn't covered by it.

The answer is True. Moses says the blessing comes “…if only you obey the LORD your God and are careful to follow all these commandments I am giving you today.” Notice the words "if only." The promise and the obeying are tied together in the same breath.

The answers are lend and rule. Verse 6 says, “…you will lend to many nations but borrow from none…” Israel would be the one with money to lend, not the one asking. That's the LORD's blessing in action. The verse goes on, “you will rule over many nations but be ruled by none.” That's the second half of the blessing, and Israel would be the one holding the reins.

The answer is to open his hand and loan what he needs. Verse 8 says, “Instead, you are to open your hand to him and freely loan him whatever he needs.” Think about a fist. You can't hold anything out with a fist, and you can't take anything either. An open hand can do both, and “freely” is the word that does the work.

The answer is giving his poor brother nothing. Moses names the wicked thought that the year of release is near, “so that you look upon your poor brother begrudgingly and give him nothing.” Moses calls it a wicked thought. It starts quietly in the heart, and it ends with an empty hand.

The answer is True. Verse 9 says, “He will cry out to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin.” The poor brother might have no one else to turn to, but he can cry out to the LORD. Moses takes that seriously, and so should we.

The answer is bless. Moses says the LORD “…will bless you in all your work and in everything to which you put your hand.” The giving is meant to be free and without a grieving heart. And the blessing covers the whole of a man's work, not just one corner of it.

The answer is free. Verse 12 says, “…in the seventh year you must set him free.” Six years of serving, then the door opens. And notice the word must, because the master doesn't get to decide otherwise.

The answer is as the LORD has blessed him. Verse 14 says, “You shall give to him as the LORD your God has blessed you.” The master gives from his flock, his threshing floor and his winepress. The size of the gift follows the size of his blessing.

The answer is that they were slaves in Egypt and the LORD redeemed them. Verse 15 says, “Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; that is why I am giving you this command today.” Israel knows from its own history what it was to be slaves and to be redeemed. Moses points them back to that when he gives the command about their servants.

The answer is that he loves his master and household and is well off. Verse 16 says he says it “because he loves you and your household and is well off with you…” He isn't stuck, since the door is open and he chooses to stay. That's a good household to be in.

The answer is for the rest of his life. Verse 17 says that after the awl goes through his ear into the door, “…he will become your servant for life.” He chose it with the door open. Once he chooses, it's for life.
The answer is False. Verse 17 ends with this line: “And treat your maidservant the same way.” Moses names the maidservant on purpose. She's treated the same way as the manservant.

The answer is twice. Verse 18 says the servant's “…six years of service were worth twice the wages of a hired hand.” So when a master frees his servant, Moses says he shouldn't regard it as a hardship. He got twice the value, and the LORD will bless him in all he does.

The answer is True. Verse 19 says, “You must set apart to the LORD your God every firstborn male produced by your herds and flocks.” Every one of them. The verse goes on to say the firstborn of the oxen aren't to be put to work, and the firstborn of the flock aren't to be sheared. Not a bad deal for an ox, while I'm over here stamping cookies all day.
